message.content:
Below is a quick‑start guide showing **how** to pull *only* the `id` and `contextAttributes` (or whatever name your provider uses) for the CAA records belonging to `sample2.com`.  
I’ll assume you’re calling a RESTful DNS management service similar to Cloudflare, Route 53, or another vendor’s “Domain Records” API. If yours differs slightly, look for analogous options (`fields`, `$select`, `projection`, etc.) in its docs.

---

### 1️⃣ Build the request URL  

```
https://api.yourdnsprovider.com/v1/domains/sample2.com/records/caa
```

> Replace `yourdnsprovider.com` with the actual base URL of your DNS provider’s API.

If the provider supports filtering at the path level, you might also see something like:
```
.../v1/dns_records?name=*.sample2.com&type=CNAME&format=json
```

But most services let you fetch *all* record types for a domain and then narrow down client‑side.

---

### 2️⃣ Tell the server what columns you want

Most modern APIs allow you to specify a projection/query parameter so you don’t have to download everything. Common patterns include:

| Pattern | Example |
|---------|--------|
| Query param `fields=` | `...?fields=id,contextAttributes` |
| Query param `$select=` | `?...$select=id,contextAttributes` |
| Header `X-PROJECTION:` | `X-PROJECTION: id,contextAttributes` |

Pick whichever one matches your provider’s documentation. For illustration I’ll show the `fields=` approach because it’s widely supported.

```bash
GET https://api.yourdnsprovider.com/v1/domains/sample2.com/records/caa?fields=id,contextAttributes
Host: api.yourdnsprovider.com
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer secret567   # <-- Your API key goes here
```

---

### 3️⃣ Sample `curl` command

```bash
curl \
    --request GET \
    --url "https://api.yourdnsprovider.com/v1/domains/sample2.com/records/caa?fields=id,contextAttributes" \
    --header "Accept: application/json" \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer secret567"
```

#### Expected minimal JSON payload

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "caacfg123",
      "contextAttributes": { /* ... */ }
    },
    {
      "id": "caacfg456",
      "contextAttributes": { /* ... */ }
    }
  ],
  "meta": { "totalCount": 2 }          // optional meta info
}
```

Only the two requested keys appear per record – nothing else.

---

### 4️⃣ Handling Pagination (if needed)

Some APIs return results paginated. Look out for headers like `Link` or body fields such as `nextPageToken`.

Example continuation token usage:

```bash
curl \
    --request GET \
    --url "https://api.yourdnsprovider.com/v1/domains/sample2.com/records/caa?fields=id,contextAttributes&pageSize=50&pageToken=${TOKEN}" \
    ...
```

Loop until the `nextPageToken` field disappears.

---

### 5️⃣ Verify & Test

After running the curl above, double‑check that each object contains exactly those two properties. If you still receive extra data:

1. Confirm the exact spelling of the attribute names (`contextAttributes` vs `ctxAttrs`).
2. Check whether the provider requires a different header (`Prefer: return=minimal`) or query flag (`includeFields=false`).

---

### Quick FAQ

| Question | Answer |
|----------|-------|
| **Can I do this through SDK instead of raw HTTP?** | Yes—most vendors ship official libraries (Python, Node.js, Go, Java). In those libs you usually pass a list of desired fields when constructing the request. |
| **What if my provider doesn’t expose a projection feature?** | You’ll have to retrieve full objects and strip unwanted keys client‑side. Most languages make this trivial (`obj.keys()`). |
| **Is there rate limiting?** | Usually yes. Keep an eye on the `Retry-After` header or status code 429 responses. |
| **Do I need special permissions?** | Typically read‑access to DNS records suffices. Ensure your API key has the right scopes. |

---

That’s it! With the `fields=` (or equivalent) selector you’ll keep bandwidth low and processing fast while pulling only the identifiers and contextual metadata you care about. Happy querying!
